chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Yaqoub al-Sarraj, who said:

We were walking with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and he wished to console a relative of his due to the death of a child. The strap of the sandal of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) snapped, so he took his sandal from his foot, then walked barefoot. Ibn Abi Yaf'ur looked at him, so he took off his own sandal from his foot, untied the strap from it, and handed it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He turned away from it as if he were displeased, then refused to accept it, then said: 'Indeed, the owner of the calamity is most deserving of patience over it.' So he walked barefoot until he entered upon the man to whom he had come to offer condolences.

key_terms.شِسْعُ: The strap or thong of a sandal
key_terms.مَوْلُودٍ: A newborn child (often implying death in this context of condolence)

ai.seo_question: What is the lesson of patience in suffering according to the Imam's reaction to his sandal strap breaking?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) demonstrates the virtue of *sabr* (patience) by walking barefoot after his sandal strap broke, deliberately rejecting his companion Ibn Abi Ya'fur's offer to repair it. This act illustrates the Shia scholarly principle that the one experiencing the calamity holds the primary right to endure it, rather than seeking immediate external relief or consolation from others. The Imam’s slight affectation of displeasure emphasizes the spiritual gravity of accepting comfort while still in the midst of the loss.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Yaqoub Al Sarraj who said,

‘We were walking along with Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> and he<sup>asws</sup> wanted to condole his<sup>asws</sup> relatives due to there being death of a child, so the strap of a sandal of Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> snapped. So he<sup>asws</sup> grabbed his<sup>asws</sup> sandal from his<sup>asws</sup> feet, then walk bare-footed. So Ibn Abu Yafour looked at him<sup>asws</sup>, so he took off his own sandal from his feet, and untied the strap from it and gave it to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>. So he<sup>asws</sup> turned away from it as if he<sup>asws</sup> was not happy, then refused to accept it, then said: ‘Indeed! The one in the difficulties is the foremost with the patience over it’. So he<sup>asws</sup> walked bare-footed until he<sup>asws</sup> came up to a man whom he gave his<sup>asws</sup> condolences’.
en.sarwar: 14. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from ibn Mahbub from Ya‘qub al-Sarraj who has said the following:

“Once we were walking with abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, to (the house of) one of his relatives for offering condolences because of the death of their child. The strap and thong of the shoe of abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, broke, so he took his shoes in his hand and began to walk barefoot. Ibn abu Ya‘fur looked at him and took his shoes off, removed its strap and thong to give it to abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, who refused to accept it as if disappointed. He (the Imam) then said, ‘The mourner has a greater responsibility to exercise patience.’ He (the Imam) continued walking barefoot until he arrived at the house of the man whom he wanted to offer condolences.’”
